title: QBism on Locality and Nonlocality
authors: John B. DeBrota, Christopher A. Fuchs, Rüdiger Schack
abstract: Recently Pienaar (2026), building on work of Cavalcanti (2021), has shown that QBism cannot always assume distinct observers' quantum-measurement outcomes---say, of Wigner and his friend---are embedded in a single spacetime. This follows from QBism's rejection of the `Absoluteness of Observed Events' assumption in the Bong et al. no-go theorem. Thus, QBism has no choice but to treat the notion of spacetime every bit as personalistic as it treats quantum states and quantum measurement outcomes. In a way, this is not a surprise to QBists, as they have taken the notion of `personalist spacetimes' to be the ansatz most compatible with their other views since at least 2009. But it does enjoin us to finally make crystal clear the sense in which QBism is a purely local interpretation of quantum mechanics despite this new theorem and despite quantum theory's age-old violation of Bell's inequalities. With the extra clarity we also hope to poise QBism for a distinctly new way to approach issues at the interface of quantum theory and gravity.
summary: This paper tackles the foundational challenge of reconciling QBism's personalist view of quantum mechanics with modern physics results suggesting that objective spacetime coordinates may not exist. The authors argue that locality must therefore be understood as an individual agent's causal structure and pattern of belief updates, allowing QM to remain local even when global spacetime assumptions fail.
main_problem: The paper addresses how QBism, a personalist interpretation of quantum mechanics, can maintain a purely local understanding despite recent theorems suggesting that distinct observers' measurement outcomes cannot be embedded in a single spacetime.
main_result: QBism maintains locality by grounding it not in shared objective spacetimes, but in the individual agent's causal structure and sequence of personal judgments (epistemic localization).
method: The authors use conceptual analysis, comparing QBism's tenets against established theorems (like Pienaar's) and analyzing the implications of rejecting the 'Absoluteness of Observed Events.'
model_or_system: The system is Quantum Mechanics analyzed through the philosophical lens of QBism. The model involves considering multiple independent agents (observers) interacting with quantum systems.
key_observables: Quantum correlations, CHSH quantity bound, and adherence to relativistic locality constraints on an agent's beliefs.
important_parameters: The distinction between objective spacetime reality versus the subjective structure of individual experience/belief updates.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that quantum theory describes decision-making processes (Bayesian updating) for an individual, and locality must be preserved at this personal level.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate probabilistic constraints on an agent's beliefs under locality in QBism and depict the full experimental scenario using each agent's personal causal diagram.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the conflict posed by modern theorems regarding spacetime embedding, then arguing that QBism must redefine locality as fundamentally epistemic (agent-specific), and finally showing how this preserves relativistic constraints.
why_interesting: While not directly about AMO systems, its deep dive into the foundations of quantum theory's relationship with spacetime is crucial for any theoretical physicist considering quantum gravity or open system dynamics where background independence is paramount.
